title: Did Sanada Yukimura Ever Actually Call Himself "Yukimura"?
description:
In Taishō 6 (1917), Tokyo Imperial University's Dai Nihon Shiryō, Series 12, Volume 19, printed a plate titled "Letter of Sanada Yukimura"; yet the letter is signed "Sa[nada] Saemon-no-suke Nobushige". Did he himself ever go by "Yukimura"?

The letters he wrote inside Osaka Castle are signed Nobushige or Saemon-no-suke; a letter from his Kudoyama years asking for shōchū is signed "Kōhaku Nobushige". He died in battle at Osaka on the 7th day of the 5th month, Keichō 20 (June 3, 1615, Gregorian calendar). A post-battle report kept by the Shimazu family (writer unknown) passes on the saying that Sanada was "the finest soldier in Japan"; the sentence itself says only "Sanada Saemon" and "Sanada", and the "Yukimura" beside it is a small note added later. The earliest text with "Yukimura" is generally held to be the war chronicle Naniwa Senki (preface dated 1672; we read an expanded copy of unknown date, further reworded in a 1928 edition). In the Tōgen Iji, compiled after Tokugawa Mitsukuni's death, the editor adds a small note: calling him Yukimura is a mistake. The Sanada family's draft genealogy gives his entry as "Yukimura", and a memo drafted in 1809 says that was the name he used after joining Osaka, yet also says no book records the change.

Conclusion: no document from his own time that we have found so far writes "Yukimura"; who first gave him that name, and why, is still unknown.

The letters are read in the Dai Nihon Shiryō transcription, not in the originals; we did not open the original Satsuhan Kyūki, an Edo-period copy of the Naniwa Senki or researchers' books, and the points on the forged letters and the battlefield commendations rest only on Japanese Wikipedia (secondhand). Dates in the narration follow the old lunar calendar; "we think" marks this channel's view; sources are listed in the references below.

The illustrations in this episode were generated with AI. The historical figures are cartoon characters, unnamed and not meant as likenesses; modern researchers and the fighting are not drawn.

Information as of 2026-10-20

sn102.text: It prints a plate: an old letter three shaku long.

sn103.text: The plate's title: Letter of Sanada Yukimura.

sn104.text: But at the end, the writer signed it himself: Nobushige.

sn105.text: Sanada Nobushige is the Sanada Yukimura we all know.

sn106.text: Title and signature: one name apart.

sn108.text: Over a month after his death, a Shimazu report left him a famous line of praise.

sn109.text: Beside that line, a later hand added two small characters.

sn110.text: After Tokugawa Mitsukuni died, Mito retainers compiled his sayings, and under Sanada's name added a note.

sn111.text: In Bunka 6, the shogunate sent questions; the Sanada drafted an answer first.

sn112.text: Did this man ever call himself Yukimura?

sn201.text: To ask him, read his letters: the one on the plate, 3rd month, 19th day, in Osaka Castle.

sn202.text: It went to his brother-in-law, Oyamada Shigemasa, and his son.

sn203.text: Life is fleeting; no one knows what tomorrow brings.

sn204.text: Please stop counting me among the living.

sn205.text: Before Nobushige: the first character of Sanada, then his title, Saemon-no-suke.

sn206.text: Then a kaō, a signature drawn as a design.

sn208.text: Muramatsu, thought to be his sister, got one that opens: someone's passing by, so a few lines.

sn209.text: It's signed only with his title, Saemon-no-suke,

sn210.text: spelled out in kana, sound by sound.

sn211.text: 2nd month, 10th day, set to hold the castle, he wrote Ishiai Jūzō more gravely:

sn212.text: Holding a castle, I'm resolved to die; we likely won't meet again in this life.

sn213.text: Signed with Sanada's first character, and Saemon-no-suke.

sn214.text: All three: the year's first 3 months

sn215.text: How did he sign before that?

sn216.text: In his years at Kudoyama, he wrote asking for drink:

sn217.text: Please send shōchū in this jar.

sn218.text: It went to a man called Sakyō; no year, signed "Kōhaku Nobushige."

sn220.text: Under two months after the in-law letter, on Keichō 20, 5th month, 7th day, he died at Osaka.

sn221.text: Researchers say his citations to his men, the day before, were on wood tabs like shōgi pieces;

sn223.text: So much for how he wrote his name; how did others write it?

sn301.text: A post-battle report kept by the Shimazu names him.

sn303.text: We read the print in that Taishō 6 sourcebook: its start is missing, and there's no signature.

sn305.text: It's filed with the records of lord Shimazu Iehisa;

sn306.text: but that doesn't mean Iehisa wrote it; the writer left no name.

sn307.text: The praise from the start is in this report:

sn308.text: Sanada, finest soldier in Japan; no old tale has his like.

sn309.text: The sentence ends with "yoshi": it is said.

sn310.text: It says it's all people talk of;

sn311.text: so is this praise the writer's own view?

sn312.text: No; the report says it records what the rank and file were saying.

sn313.text: So what does the report call him?

sn315.text: But the print adds, by "Sanada Saemon," two small characters:

sn317.text: That's the later addition from the start; the report's own words lack it.

sn318.text: Who added it is unclear; likely it was already there when the report was copied.

sn401.text: Generally held the earliest: the Osaka war chronicle Naniwa Senki.

sn402.text: Its preface is dated Kanbun 12, 57 years after the Osaka battles.

sn403.text: It says: Saemon-no-suke Yukimura, second son of Sanada Masayuki, lord of Ueda Castle.

sn404.text: "Yuki" is in father Masayuki's name, and son Yukimasa's;

sn405.text: but why Yukimura, the book never says.

sn406.text: So people called him that the year of the preface?

sn407.text: Not yet. That preface was written for the two original authors.

sn408.text: We read a later, expanded copy.

sn409.text: When did the expander set to work?

sn410.text: He gave no year; reset in Shōwa 3, it was reworded.

sn411.text: Whether the original had Yukimura, we can't tell.

sn412.text: Is there a record with a firm date?

sn413.text: Yes. In Genroku 13, 12th month, Tokugawa Mitsukuni of Mito died; by the Western calendar, early 1701.

sn414.text: The book of sayings from the start: the Tōgen Iji, compiled after his death.

sn415.text: It records Mitsukuni speaking of Sanada, calling him "Nobuyori."

sn416.text: Right under that name, the editor added a small note:

sn418.text: That's the editor speaking, not Mitsukuni.

sn419.text: So Yukimura had spread enough that someone had to correct it.

sn420.text: But does their "Nobuyori" match his letters?

sn421.text: No; "Nobuyori" appears nowhere in his letters.

sn422.text: The later essay collection Okinagusa read this as: Mitsukuni himself showed Yukimura was wrong.

sn423.text: We think even "who said Yukimura was wrong" got rewritten once.

sn424.text: Outsiders said Yukimura was wrong; how did the Sanada record him?

sn501.text: The Sanada family's later draft genealogy gives his entry as "Yukimura."

sn503.text: The draft says: first named Nobushige; on Mount Kōya, called Kōhaku.

sn504.text: The opening question came in Bunka 6, 11th month: the chief inspector asked of the old genealogy.

sn505.text: One asked: was Nobushige his first name?

sn506.text: The Sanada drafted a memo on how to answer: yes, Nobushige was his first name.

sn507.text: It also notes that an earlier report listed both names, Nobushige and Yukimura.

sn509.text: Say it was the name he used only after leaving the family for the Osaka side;

sn511.text: This is only a memo; what was actually sent, we haven't seen.

sn512.text: Remember the three Keichō 20 letters from Osaka Castle?

sn513.text: Signed Nobushige, or his title Saemon-no-suke; not one says Yukimura.

sn515.text: his name change to Yukimura is in no book.

sn516.text: Is there any letter he signed "Yukimura"?

sn517.text: Two copies survive, no originals; researchers judge both to be forgeries.

sn519.text: In Meiji 44, nearly 300 years after his death, Tatsukawa Bunko put out volume 5: Chibō Sanada Yukimura.

sn520.text: Price: 25 sen; the same ad lists Ikkyū Zenji and a tale of Mito Kōmon.

sn521.text: Storytellers and novels made "Sanada Yukimura" a name the whole nation knew.

sn523.text: Its contents read: "Sanada Yukimura, general of Osaka";

sn524.text: even the shōchū letter's margin note says: Yukimura wants shōchū.

sn526.text: We think that plate's title records just what that era called him.

sn527.text: So, our opening question: did he ever call himself Yukimura?

sn528.text: Who first called him that, and why, is still unknown today;

sn529.text: but whether he used it, records can answer.

sn530.text: No document from his time found so far says "Yukimura"; this case: filed.
